prompt: Let $f(x) = x^4 - 4x^3$. Which statement about its critical points is true?

choices.label: $f$ has a local minimum at $x = 3$ and no local extremum at $x = 0$.
$f$ has a local maximum at $x = 0$ and a local minimum at $x = 3$.
$f$ has local minima at both $x = 0$ and $x = 3$.

hint: Find the critical numbers from $f'(x) = 4x^3 - 12x^2 = 4x^2(x - 3)$. Then check whether $f'$ actually changes sign at each one.

hints.text: Find the critical numbers from $f'(x) = 4x^3 - 12x^2 = 4x^2(x - 3)$. Then check whether $f'$ actually changes sign at each one.

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Warm up with $y = x^3$: its derivative $3x^2$ is zero at $x = 0$ but positive on both sides, so $x = 0$ is NOT an extremum. A squared factor in $f'$ is the warning sign.
Here $4x^2 \ge 0$ always, so the sign of $f'$ is the sign of $(x - 3)$: negative for $x < 3$ (including both sides of $0$), positive for $x > 3$.
No sign change at $0$ (no extremum); $-$ to $+$ at $3$ (local min). Choice A.

explanation: $f'(x) = 4x^3 - 12x^2 = 4x^2(x - 3)$, so the critical numbers are $x = 0$ and $x = 3$.
Sign of $f'$: the factor $4x^2$ is never negative, so $f'$ has the sign of $x - 3$. That is negative on $(-\infty, 0)$ and on $(0, 3)$, positive on $(3, \infty)$.
At $x = 0$ there is no sign change, so no extremum — the graph just flattens momentarily (it is an inflection point). At $x = 3$ the sign goes $-$ to $+$: a local minimum, $f(3) = -27$. Choice A.

alternativeExplanations.title: Second Derivative Test, and where it fails
steps: At $x = 0$: $f''(0) = 0$, so the test is INCONCLUSIVE — it does not say "no extremum," it says "look harder."
Looking harder (the sign chart of $f'$) shows no sign change at $0$. Always fall back to the first-derivative sign chart when $f'' = 0$.
